newsitem.title: GERMANY: German metal employers cornered by pay deal.
newsitem.headline: German metal employers cornered by pay deal.

text.p: Germany's metal and engineering employers on Sunday criticised a regional wage deal reached in the sector last week would but admitted it now set the tone for further negotiations in other regions.

Gesamtmetall, the metal and engineering industry employers federation, had earlier held a board meeting to discuss a pay deal in the state of Lower Saxony that failed to implement a new law allowing empoyers to cut worker sick payments.

The deal followed mass protests and the threat of all-out strikes by the powerful IG Metall trade union over the last two months against a new law cutting sick pay from 100 percent of salary to 80 percent.

Gesamtmetall president Werner Stumpfe told journalists after the meeting that the Lower Saxony wage deal had been "very disappointing" in that it would not allow most employers in the industry to reduce their costs.
"But realistic as we are, we recognise that this agreement leaves the other regions no chance of distancing themselves from it in any significant respect," Stumpfe told a news briefing.

Although the Lower Saxony deal applies to just 90,000 out of the three million-plus workers in Germany's metal and engineering industries, it was the first agreement to be reached since the collapse of national wage talks some weeks ago.
Officials for IG Metall, Germany's largest trade union, had earlier last week hailed the deal as a victory for workers and urged other regions to agree similar packages.
The Lower Saxony wage pact was however seen by employers as a major set-back, increasing their overall costs for the next two years.
Under the deal, workers will receive a wage rise of 1.5 percent in 1997 and 2.5 percent in 1998, for which union negotiators in return agreed to lower holiday and other bonuses.
But Stumpfe said the deal would raise average labour costs by nearly one percent in 1997, rising to nearly two percent in 1998.
Other negotiations are now due in other states in the country, including much larger regions such as North Rhine-Westphalia, the core of Germany's steel-making industry.

Stumpfe however denied an earlier IG Metall statement that a deal similar to the Lower Saxony pact had been reached for 300,000 workers in the southern state of Baden-Wuerttemberg, saying talks were still at a preliminary stage.

The cut in sick pay to 80 percent is allowed under austerity laws passed by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government this autumn to boost job creation in Germany, suffering from record post-unification unemployment of four million.
Protests against the law have also taken place in Germany's banking and chemical sectors.
